claim: The study reports improved automated open-source methodology for head-fixed mesoscale cortical imaging and/or behavioral training of home cage mice using Raspberry Pi-based hardware.
source: We report improved automated open-source methodology for head-fixed mesoscale cortical imaging and/or behavioral training of home cage mice using Raspberry Pi-based hardware.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the work.

claim: Staged partial and probabilistic restraint allows mice to adjust to self-initiated headfixation over 3 weeks' time with ~50% participation rate.
source: Staged partial and probabilistic restraint allows mice to adjust to self-initiated headfixation over 3 weeks' time with ~50% participation rate.
evidence: This is a direct statement in the abstract describing a key methodological finding.

claim: The system supports a cue-based behavioral licking task monitored by a capacitive touch-sensor water spout.
source: We support a cue-based behavioral licking task monitored by a capacitive touch-sensor water spout.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a feature of the system.

claim: While automatically head-fixed, spontaneous, movement-triggered, or licking task-evoked GCaMP6 cortical signals are acquired.
source: While automatically head-fixed, we acquire spontaneous, movement-triggered, or licking task-evoked GCaMP6 cortical signals.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a capability of the system.

claim: Mice were trained to suppress licking and wait for cues that marked the delivery of water.
source: Mice were trained to suppress licking and wait for cues that marked the delivery of water.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a behavioral training outcome.

claim: Correct rewarded go-trials were associated with widespread activation of midline and lateral barrel cortex areas following a vibration cue and delayed frontal and lateral motor cortex activation.
source: Correct rewarded go-trials were associated with widespread activation of midline and lateral barrel cortex areas following a vibration cue and delayed frontal and lateral motor cortex activation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the brain imaging data.

claim: Cortical GCaMP signals predicted trial success and correlated strongly with trial-outcome dependent body movements.
source: Cortical GCaMP signals predicted trial success and correlated strongly with trial-outcome dependent body movements.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding from the analysis.

claim: Automation has been extended to complex headfixed visual tasks with a relatively good success rate in mice (Aoki et al., 2017) and headfixed rats (Scott et al., 2013).
source: Automation has been extended to complex headfixed visual tasks with a relatively good success rate in mice (Aoki et al., 2017) and headfixed rats (Scott et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The work described in Aoki et al in mice did not autonomously gather longitudinal mesoscale brain imaging data, or use with animals in a group and relied on daily supervised 2-photon imaging.
source: While the work described in Aoki et al in mice was impressive for introducing a complex visual task to home cage training, this work did not autonomously gather longitudinal mesoscale brain imaging data, or use with animals in a group and relied on daily supervised 2-photon imaging.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The lab and others have begun to automate the acquisition of mesoscale functional brain imaging (Murphy et al., 2016) and motor actions data using compact and cost-effective Linux-based Raspberry Pi or other single board computers (Ardesch et al., 2017; Silasi et al., 2018; Woodard et al., 2017).
source: Recently, our lab and others have begun to automate the acquisition of mesoscale functional brain imaging (Murphy et al., 2016) and motor actions data using compact and cost-effective Linux-based Raspberry Pi or other single board computers (Ardesch et al., 2017; Silasi et al., 2018; Woodard et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The work extends previous automated analysis of animal behaviors within home cages (Bollu et al., 2019; Robinson et al., 2013; Robinson and Riedel, 2014; Robinson et al., 2018) to the more complex brain circuit level analysis during behavioral tasks in combination with mesoscale imaging.
source: This work extends previous automated analysis of animal behaviors within home cages (Bollu et al., 2019; Robinson et al., 2013; Robinson and Riedel, 2014; Robinson et al., 2018) to the more complex brain circuit level analysis during behavioral tasks in combination with mesoscale imaging.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work and describes the contribution of the current work.

claim: Automated mouse (Murphy et al., 2016) and rat brain imaging has recently been described (Scott et al., 2013).
source: While automated mouse (Murphy et al., 2016) and rat brain imaging has recently been described (Scott et al., 2013), the work presented here provides a significant improvement over the initial mouse-based designs (Murphy et al., 2016) and to led to higher rates of head fixation, greater data throughput, and coupling to a behavioral task.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The work presented here provides a significant improvement over the initial mouse-based designs (Murphy et al., 2016) and led to higher rates of head fixation, greater data throughput, and coupling to a behavioral task.
source: While automated mouse (Murphy et al., 2016) and rat brain imaging has recently been described (Scott et al., 2013), the work presented here provides a significant improvement over the initial mouse-based designs (Murphy et al., 2016) and to led to higher rates of head fixation, greater data throughput, and coupling to a behavioral task.
evidence: This is a direct statement comparing the current work to prior work with citation.

claim: The study tested 44 adult male GCaMP6 transgenic mice and an additional cohort of 8 female mice.
source: We have tested 44 adult male GCaMP6 transgenic mice (Table 1 and Figure 3) and an additional cohort of 8 female mice that were trained for ~7 h/day that yielded similar levels of participation (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and references Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: Female mice trained for ~7 h/day yielded similar levels of participation to male mice.
source: We have tested 44 adult male GCaMP6 transgenic mice (Table 1 and Figure 3) and an additional cohort of 8 female mice that were trained for ~7 h/day that yielded similar levels of participation (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and references Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mesoscale widefield in vivo imaging maps activation of cortex over a field-of-view that can extend bilaterally from olfactory bulb to visual cortex (Mohajerani et al., 2013).
source: Mesoscale widefield in vivo imaging maps activation of cortex over a field-of-view that can extend bilaterally from olfactory bulb to visual cortex (Mohajerani et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Wide field imaging is typically done with larger focal volume (~2–3 mm) to image curved brain surfaces and lower spatial resolution (pixels binned to ~32–49 μm) to sum more photons over a larger area (Lim et al., 2012).
source: In contrast to single cell imaging needing high resolution in the X-Y plane and in depth, wide field imaging is typically done with larger focal volume (~2–3 mm) to image curved brain surfaces and lower spatial resolution (pixels binned to ~32–49 μm) to sum more photons over a larger area (Lim et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The intrinsically large depth of field and reduced resolution provided by the small lenses employed by compact cameras such as the Raspberry Pi Camera Module are not expected to degrade signals.
source: Thus, the intrinsically large depth of field and reduced resolution provided by the small lenses employed by compact cameras such as the Raspberry Pi Camera Module (Figure 1B,C) are not expected to degrade signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of wide field imaging and the camera hardware.

claim: The system would be suitable for training animals on complex headfixed tasks where imaging could be performed using parallel manual headfixation and advanced two-photon imaging or electrophysiological procedures (Chen et al., 2017; Le Merre et al., 2018; Prsa et al., 2017), as was already elegantly applied by others (Aoki et al., 2017).
source: While we emphasize single photon mesoscale widefield imaging within these cages, our system would also be suitable for training animals on complex headfixed tasks where imaging could be performed using parallel manual headfixation and advanced two-photon imaging or electrophysiological procedures (Chen et al., 2017; Le Merre et al., 2018; Prsa et al., 2017), as was already elegantly applied by others (Aoki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about potential applications supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The initial design (Murphy et al., 2016) employed electromagnetic solenoids.
source: The initial design (Murphy et al., 2016) employed electromagnetic solenoids.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Using the electromagnetic solenoid system, it was impossible to control the degree of restraint and it produced a significant audible and vibration stimulus.
source: Using this system, it was impossible to control the degree of restraint and it produced a significant audible and vibration stimulus.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the prior system.

claim: A servo-based system (Hitec HF-645 or HSB-9475SH) was developed which allows variable degrees of headfixation with an initial training period where mice were loosely headfixed.
source: As an improvement to this, we developed a servo-based system (Hitec HF-645 or HSB-9475SH; use the latter for even less noise and vibration) which allows variable degrees of headfixation with an initial training period where mice were loosely headfixed (achieved by controlling the servo travel) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the improved system design.

claim: Loose headfixation allows mice to move significantly and grow accustomed to restraint.
source: Loose headfixation allows mice to move significantly and grow accustomed to restraint.
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for the loose headfixation approach.

claim: The loose fixation period, along with the less jarring mechanics has resulted in significantly higher rates of headfixation than previous work (Murphy et al., 2016).
source: This loose fixation period, along with the less jarring mechanics has resulted in significantly higher rates of headfixation than previous work (Murphy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct comparison to prior work with citation.

claim: In a total of 5 improved cages that were tested, an average of 28+−17 head fixations per day per animal was observed for a subset of animals tested (23/44) that exhibited high rates of headfixation.
source: In a total of 5 improved cages that were tested, we observed average of 28+−17 head fixations per day per animal for a subset of animals tested (23/44) that exhibited high rates of headfixation (for supplemental database of all mice see methods and repositories).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a quantitative finding.

claim: The time headfixed for the 23 good performers averaged 18+−13 min/day per animal.
source: The time headfixed for these 23 good performers averaged 18+−13 min/day per animal (Table 1, behavioral data from all mice are available in an online database, see methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a quantitative finding referencing Table 1.

claim: In the current cage the cut-off for a poor performer was <20 min of total headfixation time, while good performers averaged 15.8+−19.9 hr (summed time over all daily sessions).
source: In the current cage the cut-off for a poor performer was <20 min of total headfixation time, while good performers averaged 15.8+−19.9 hr (summed time over all daily sessions).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a quantitative finding.

claim: Assuming a session length of ~40 s, taking the top 50% of headfixing mice would result in an average of 6.5+−4 min of daily data acquisition or training per mouse using the initial design.
source: Assuming a session length of ~40 s, which was the typical range in the previous system (Murphy et al., 2016), taking the top 50% of headfixing mice would result in an average of 6.5+−4 min of daily data acquisition or training per mouse using the initial design.
evidence: This is a calculation based on data from the prior system with citation.

claim: In the improved cages, animals exhibit much longer daily durations of head fixation which leads to more spontaneous brain activity imaging data, but also the possibility to assess mesoscale functional circuits using GCaMP imaging as animal's train in simple detection or choice tasks.
source: In the improved cages, animals exhibit much longer daily durations of head fixation which leads to more spontaneous brain activity imaging data, but also the possibility to assess mesoscale functional circuits using GCaMP imaging as animal's train in simple detection or choice tasks.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the improved system.

claim: In total 34,114 videos of brain activity in headfix sessions were recorded, where 29,097 were task related.
source: In total we were able to record 34,114 videos of brain activity in headfix sessions, where 29,097 were task related.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a quantitative finding.

claim: An additional 5423 sessions were recorded from a cage with 8 female mice during daily lab-based 7 h/day training where 5 advanced to high levels of participation.
source: An additional 5423 sessions were recorded from a cage with 8 female mice during daily lab-based 7 h/day training where 5 advanced to high levels of participation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of a quantitative finding referencing Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The improved cage employs infrared beam breaks to determine mouse position for fixation rather than electrical contact with the fixation bar where buildup of insulating dirt/oil can reduce sensitivity.
source: Moreover, the improved cage employs infrared beam breaks (Figure 1C) to determine mouse position for fixation rather than, as in the previous version (Murphy et al., 2016), electrical contact with the fixation bar where buildup of insulating dirt/oil can reduce sensitivity.
evidence: This is a direct statement about an improvement in the system design with citation to prior work.

claim: A capacitance-based lick detector based around the MPR-121 was employed previously in a mouse tapered beam assay (Ardesch et al., 2017).
source: A capacitance-based lick detector based around the MPR-121 that we employed previously in a mouse tapered beam assay (Ardesch et al., 2017) provides a system to confirm that mice are reaching the water spout and that they can register an output during a licking-based behavioral task.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The study implemented a relational database to relate brain activity to more than 7.5 million behavioral events.
source: To relate the brain activity to the (currently) more than 7.5 million behavioral events (such as licking) and training circumstances we also implemented a relational database, allowing us to effectively analyze the data by pipelining plots and statistical tests to adaptive queries (see Materials and methods for how to access the database where we share all behavioral data collected).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data management approach.

claim: For initial training 8–10 post-surgical male mice with RFID tags (Bolaños et al., 2017) and transcranial windows that were at least 45 days of age (Silasi et al., 2016) were kept in their double training cage for several weeks with ad libitum water from a bottle.
source: For initial training 8–10 post-surgical male mice (2 cages of 10 and 3 cages of 8 mice) with RFID tags (Bolaños et al., 2017) and transcranial windows that were at least 45 days of age (Silasi et al., 2016) were kept in their double training cage for several weeks with ad libitum water from a bottle (Figure 2A, and see protocol steps in Methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol with citations to prior work.

claim: A group of female 8 mice was also trained in a similar manner.
source: A group of female 8 mice was also trained in a similar manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol referencing Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice were weighed on the subsequent day and this weight is the baseline by which 15% wt loss criteria were determined (for water supplementation).
source: Mice were weighed on the subsequent day and this weight is the baseline by which 15% wt loss criteria were determined (for water supplementation).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: After determining that the majority of mice entered the chamber, the water spout was progressively moved until it is 7–10 mm from the back wall of the headfixation tube (typically this takes 5–18 days).
source: After determining that the majority of mice entered the chamber (by reading RFID tags and lick detection) we progressively moved the water spout until it is 7–10 mm from the back wall of the headfixation tube (typically this takes 5–18 days) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: Once the infrared beams are broken a no-fix trial is initiated and the mouse receives up to 5 large water rewards for just getting at the end of the tube.
source: Once the infrared beams are broken a no-fix trial is initiated the mouse receives up to 5 large water rewards for just getting at the end of the tube.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: Initially a 50% probability of loose headfixation was set.
source: Initially we set a 50% probability of loose headfixation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: Over 7–10 days the fixation mechanism was gradually tightened until the headbar was tightly pressed against the metal reinforcement at the end of the rails.
source: Next, over 7–10 days we gradually tightened the fixation mechanism (increase servo forward travel, fixed setting) until the headbar was tightly pressed against the metal reinforcement at the end of the rails.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: During this period the probability of headfixation was gradually increased until mice were fully headfixed 75–90% of the time for about 19–45 s.
source: Additionally, during this period we gradually increased the probability of headfixation until mice were fully headfixed 75–90% of the time for about 19–45 s.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: Headfixing probability was never set to 100% as a potential safety mechanism allowing animals that for some reason could not un-break the IR beams in time to be prevented from re-fixation.
source: Headfixing probability was never set to 100% as a potential safety mechanism allowing animals that for some reason could not un-break the IR beams in time (parameter called skedaddle time in software) to be prevented from re-fixation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol and safety considerations.

claim: A text messaging service was setup to send automated warnings if a mouse was present in the headfixing tube for longer than 600–800 s.
source: A text messaging service was also setup to send automated warnings if a mouse was present in the headfixing tube for longer than 600–800 s.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a safety feature of the system.

claim: Plotting entry rates, time headfixed, and headfixing rates for all mice tested indicated a peak of early entries just after the mice were placed in the cage.
source: Plotting entry rates, time headfixed, and headfixing rates for all mice tested indicated a peak of early entries just after the mice were placed in the cage (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a finding referencing Figure 3A.

claim: At early times of training (even in the second day in the cage) mice were actively licking the waterspout.
source: At these early times of training (even in the second day in the cage) mice were actively licking the waterspout (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a finding referencing Figure 3B.

claim: There was a transition to headfixation which began with a loose restraint and was progressively tightened over 4–7 days to the point where mesoscale imaging data could be acquired with minimal motion artifact.
source: This was followed by a transition to headfixation which began with a loose restraint and was progressively tightened over 4–7 days to the point where mesoscale imaging data could be acquired with minimal motion artifact (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a finding referencing Figure 3C.

claim: The mice entered less frequently after the first 10 days of headfixation once they transitioned from entrance rewards to receiving multiple task rewards.
source: The graphs illustrated that the mice entered less frequently after the first 10 days of headfixation once they transitioned from entrance rewards to receiving multiple task rewards (Figure 3A) and collectively the mice of the 5 cages could yield up to 4 hr headfixed training or imaging a day (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a finding referencing Figure 3A and 3D.

claim: Collectively the mice of the 5 cages could yield up to 4 hr headfixed training or imaging a day.
source: The graphs illustrated that the mice entered less frequently after the first 10 days of headfixation once they transitioned from entrance rewards to receiving multiple task rewards (Figure 3A) and collectively the mice of the 5 cages could yield up to 4 hr headfixed training or imaging a day (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a finding referencing Figure 3D.

claim: Mice headfixed repeatedly over short time intervals with an average median interval of 5.8+- 4.1 s.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Murphy et al., 2016) mice headfixed repeatedly over short time intervals (Figure 4A,B, red) with an average median interval of 5.8+- 4.1 s (Figure 4C, red line).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a finding referencing Figure 4 and citing prior work.

claim: Plotting histograms for the time interval between different mice headfixing showed short interval repetitions with a second different mouse: average median interval of 305+- 575 s indicating linked behaviors between mice.
source: Surprisingly, plotting histograms for the time interval between different mice headfixing (Figure 4A,B, black) also showed short interval repetitions with a second different mouse: average median interval of 305+- 575 s indicating linked behaviors between mice.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a finding referencing Figure 4.

claim: Plotting the median separately for each group showed large differences in inter-mouse headfixing times between cages, indicating potential group dynamics.
source: Plotting the median separately for each group (Figure 4C, black line) showed large differences in inter-mouse headfixing times between cages, indicating potential group dynamics, however given the small sample size of cages (n = 5) we did not investigate statistically.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a finding referencing Figure 4C.

claim: Cluster analysis indicated most headfixes occurred in large temporal groups that could involve 1 or several mice.
source: Cluster analysis indicated most headfixes occurred in large temporal groups that could involve 1 or several mice (Figure 4C,D,E,F).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a finding referencing Figure 4.

claim: Plotting headfix events on a 24 hr timescale indicated that headfixes are not done randomly, but often form dense clusters of activity and 69+−11% of headfixes were performed at night (n = 5 cages); with the exception of cage 6 tested during the day only.
source: Plotting headfix events on a 24 hr timescale with each day stacked on the Y-axis (Figure 4D,F) indicated that headfixes are not done randomly, but often form dense clusters of activity and 69+−11% of headfixes were performed at night (n = 5 cages); with the exception of cage 6 tested during the day only.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a finding referencing Figure 4D and 4F.

claim: Testing the time interval between headfixes revealed that they were not uniformly or normally distributed across a day (Anderson-Darling test; test statistic 14137, critical value for 1% level is 1.092, indicating a very low probability of normality) consistent with the temporal clusters observed.
source: Testing the time interval between headfixes revealed that they were not uniformly or normally distributed across a day (Anderson-Darling test; test statistic 14137, critical value for 1% level is 1.092, indicating a very low probability of normality) consistent with the temporal clusters we observed.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a statistical finding.

claim: The first stage of task training is called lick suppression where water is dispensed only when licking is withheld for 0.5–2 s.
source: Therefore, the first stage of task training is called lick suppression where water is dispensed only when licking is withheld for 0.5–2 s.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: A 0.5 s mean random interval was added to the lick suppression time to help ensure mice wait for a cue rather than use internal timing.
source: We added a 0.5 s mean random interval to this time to help ensure mice wait for a cue rather than use internal timing (Figure 5A); see group data on licking counts for all mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: Licking at an inappropriate time was met with auditory feedback: a tone of 0.3 kHz was given to provide immediate feedback using piezo buzzer.
source: Licking at an inappropriate time was met with auditory feedback: a tone of 0.3 kHz was given to provide immediate feedback using piezo buzzer (Adafruit product #1739).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: Once lick suppression training was initiated mice were given a vibratory cue (500 ms continuous or pulsed 3 × 200 ms, 100 ms duty cycle) to signal that water will be dispensed after the lick suppression period is met.
source: Once lick suppression training was initiated mice were given a vibratory (Adafruit Vibe motor #1201) cue (500 ms continuous or pulsed 3 × 200 ms, 100 ms duty cycle) to signal that water will be dispensed after the lick suppression period is met.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: In cages 1 and 2 lick suppression began during headfixation, while in cages 3–5 it was started 2–4 days prior to loose headfixation.
source: In cages 1 and 2 lick suppression began during headfixation, while in cages 3–5 it was started 2–4 days prior to loose headfixation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: Over time the period of lick suppression was increased to 2 s (+- 0.5 s random interval) and water would only be dispensed when a mouse licks within a time window after the cue.
source: Over time the period of lick suppression was increased to 2 s (+- 0.5 s random interval) and water would only be dispensed when a mouse licks within a time window after the cue.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: A self-timed delay period after the cue (0.3–1.1 s) was added where mice should not lick between the cue and the end of the delay period.
source: As the goal was to extend training to a go and no-go task (Gilad et al., 2018), where mice will need to process and discriminate between two similar vibratory cues, we also added a self-timed delay period after the cue (0.3–1.1 s). Mice should not lick between the cue and the end of the delay period.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol with citation.

claim: When using the delay period, water was delivered following go-stimuli if the licking response occurred between the end of the delay period and 1.25 s after that.
source: When using the delay period, water was delivered following go-stimuli if the licking response occurred between the end of the delay period and 1.25 s after that (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: Initially, mice licked immediately after the cue and these errors were not rewarded and these task outcomes were termed lick early (coded −4) trials and signaled by auditory feedback.
source: Initially, mice licked immediately after the cue and these errors were not rewarded and these task outcomes were termed lick early (coded −4) trials and signaled by auditory feedback using the same tone as for lick suppression (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol and task outcomes.

claim: Over time the delay period is increased from 300 ms by ~50–100 ms a day to an eventual 1100 ms.
source: Over time the delay period is increased from 300 ms by ~50–100 ms a day to an eventual 1100 ms.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the training protocol.

claim: Analysis of success rate data for the Go detection task indicated that most mice actually had higher success rates while head-fixed than non-head fixed (RM 2WAY ANOVA, p=0.0026, n = 8).
source: Surprisingly, analysis of success rate data for the Go detection task indicated that most mice actually had higher success rates while head-fixed than non-head fixed (RM 2WAY ANOVA, p=0.0026, n = 8) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a statistical finding referencing Figure 5C.

claim: All data on task performance presented in Table 1 and used to calculate reported d' were calculated for fully headfixed trials.
source: All data on task performance presented in Table 1 and used to calculate reported d' were calculated for fully headfixed trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data analysis approach.

claim: The ratio of success rate for day and night was similar across mice (1.03+0.17, t-test: p=0.40, maximum ratios: 0.56 and 1.39, n = 21 mice that performed the go-task under headfixation for more than 10 days).
source: Overall, the ratio of success rate for day and night was similar across mice (1.03+0.17, t-test: p=0.40, maximum ratios: 0.56 and 1.39, n = 21 mice that performed the go-task under headfixation for more than 10 days).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a statistical finding.

claim: No instances of a significant day-night preference were found (p>0.05), except M985 that had a very low success rate.
source: We also assessed whether any individual mouse had a consistent day-night preference (t-test for each mouse using day/night success ratios for each day) and found no instances of a significant bias (p>0.05), except M985 that had a very low success rate (see Table 1) and therefore produced a very inconsistent daily day and night success rate ratio.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a statistical finding.

claim: Mice were first trained on the go detection task and over the first 1–4 days could already pause and lick correctly (Go=+2 code) after the delay period.
source: Mice were first trained on the go detection task and over the first 1–4 days could already pause and lick correctly (Go=+2 code) after the delay period.
evidence: This is a direct statement about a training outcome.

claim: Even early in training there was relatively little non-rewarded early licking (Go=-4 code for early licking in the go trial).
source: Even early in training there was relatively little non-rewarded early licking (Go=-4 code for early licking in the go trial (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a training outcome referencing Figure 6B.

claim: The proportion of early licks (Go=-4) and ignored cues (Go=-2) was further reduced after 55–68 days of training even with a much longer delay period of up to 1 s.
source: The proportion of early licks (Go=-4) and ignored cues (Go=-2) was further reduced after 55–68 days of training even with a much longer delay period of up to 1 s (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a training outcome referencing Figure 6C.

source: No-go trials were introduced after 14 days of go-training and initially mice had trouble distinguishing the 2 trial types and would lick after the delay period as in a go-trial leading to a −1 code error (or −3 when licking early during the delay period for a no-go trial).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a training outcome.

claim: Throughout training, there was marked reduction in licking after the no-go cue as the mice learned to distinguish the two stimuli.
source: Throughout training, there was marked reduction in licking after the no-go cue as the mice learned to distinguish the two stimuli (No-go trial correct rejection is No-go=+1) (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement about a training outcome referencing Figure 6.

claim: The sample sizes for the no-go task were relatively small (n = 10 mice) and only 5 of these mice had a sensitivity index (d') greater than 2 during their best task training days.
source: While we appreciate the power of a choice task, the sample sizes for the no-go task were relatively small (n = 10 mice) and only 5 of these mice had a sensitivity index (also called d') greater than 2 during their best task training days.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size and performance.

claim: d' is a z-transformed measure of the discrimination between go and no-go stimuli (hit rate (correct)z – false alarm (incorrect)z), with a value of 0 corresponding to no discrimination.
source: d' is a z-transformed measure of the discrimination between go and no-go stimuli (hit rate (correct)z – false alarm (incorrect)z), with a value of 0 corresponding to no discrimination.
evidence: This is a definition of a statistical measure.

claim: The 5 mice that were good performers had a d' that averaged 1.37+−0.53 over their days of testing and they reached a maximal daily d' that averaged 2.3 +−0.52 and ranged from 1.9 to 3.21.
